Customers.CustomerSummary: Customer A was a 49-year-old accountant who opened an account with Orlando at Spartan in June 2016. Between August and November 2018, Orlando engaged in excessive trading in Customer A's account resulting in a turnover rate of 20 and a cost-to-equity ratio of 87%, significantly above the guidelines of 6 and 20% respectively. This trading generated $38,513 in total costs ($36,777 in commissions), while causing $80,072 in realized losses. While Customer A's stated investment objective was speculation, the extreme level of trading was unsuitable given the high costs and significant losses. Since this trading occurred before Regulation BI went into effect (June 30, 2020), the violation falls under FINRA Rule 2111 (suitability) rather than a Care Obligation violation.

Case Information.Type of Document: Letter of Acceptance, Waiver, and Consent (AWC)

OverallSummary: This case involves Troy Allen Orlando, a former General Securities Representative, who engaged in excessive trading in five customers' accounts between January 2018 and November 2020 while registered with Spartan Capital Securities, LLC and Worden Capital Management LLC. The excessive trading violated both FINRA Rule 2111 (suitability) for the period before June 30, 2020, and the Best Interest Obligation under Regulation BI for the period after June 30, 2020. Orlando exercised de facto control over all five accounts as customers relied on and followed his recommendations. Analysis of the excessive trading was based on two key metrics: (1) turnover rates ranging from 20 to 93 (far exceeding the guideline threshold of 6), and (2) cost-to-equity ratios ranging from 87% to 279% (far exceeding the guideline threshold of 20%). The five customers affected included: (1) a 49-year-old accountant who suffered $80,072 in losses and paid $38,513 in trading costs; (2) a 63-year-old real estate executive who suffered $12,818 in losses and paid $24,988 in trading costs; (3) a 67-year-old car dealership owner with limited investment knowledge who suffered $37,998 in losses and paid $65,934 in trading costs; (4) a 48-year-old engineer who suffered $40,710 in losses and paid $62,281 in trading costs; and (5) a 71-year-old truck salesman who suffered $26,852 in losses and paid $40,082 in trading costs. While all customers had designated speculation as their investment objective, the extreme level of trading was not in their best interest and violated regulatory obligations. The total realized losses across all five accounts amounted to $198,450, with total trading costs of $231,798. As a result of these violations, Orlando was suspended for 20 months and ordered to pay $58,082.50 in restitution (to Customers A and B, as Customers C, D, and E had already obtained an arbitration award against Worden).
